content.title: Where can I find the exact reference in Ezekiel 25:17 that Jules Winnfield in Pulp Fiction quotes?
content.text: Where can I find the exact reference in Ezekiel 25:17 that Jules Winnfield in Pulp Fiction quotes?Answered by · Upvoted by , MBA Movies, University of California, Santa Cruz · Author has 1.2K answers and 41.1M answer views · Mar 4, 2024 · Let’s be clear, you cannot find the Jules Winfield quote from Ezekiel 25:17 in the actual Bible. While Ezekiel 25:17 is very much a real Book, chapter and verse, it doesn’t say what Jules Winfield says on screen. Quentin Tarantino took “artistic liberties,” so to speak, when he drafted Jules’ “badass” speech. While the speech sounds suitably fire and brimstone, Tarantino was looking for the Bible to say something it didn’t. He was looking for it to boil a number of prominent Judeo-Christian themes down to a single memorable quote, in a way which the Bible never actually does.(Jules Winfield, a profane, cold-blooded hitman who has the perfect Bible quote for his killings? Cool for the film, but not really real.) When Tarantino couldn’t find an apt verse he took a real passage that said a very small bit of what he wanted it to say, pulled it out of context and greatly expanded and altered it to incorporate all the themes he wanted Jules Winfield to be pondering in the film. It was kind of a brilliant technique. Many viewers to this day believe actor Samuel L Jackson is quoting the actual Bible when he isn’t.(It turns out Jules Winfield isn’t really religious, at all. He just considered the quote a cold-blooded thing to say before killing someone. But the “miracle” of surviving being shot at himself, gets him thinking about the quote he’s been using in a new way.) Unless viewers have done a tremendous amount of Bible study, and could tell how off the quote sounds (and it does sound off, by the way), they’d have no reason to doubt the quote despite it being mainly invented. And few who hadn’t done a lot of Bible study would bother to, you know, just grab a copy of the Bible and check to see if the quote is accurate. The speech Jules delivers is the following: “The path of the righteous man is beset on all sides by the inequities of the selfish and the tyranny of evil men. Blessed is he who, in the name of charity and good will, shepherds the weak through the valley of darkness, for he is truly his brother's keeper and the finder of lost children. And I will strike down upon thee with great vengeance and furious anger those who attempt to poison and destroy my brothers. And you will know my name is the Lord when I lay my vengeance upon thee.” But it just isn’t in the Bible, at all.(By this point in the film, Jules has finally rethought his life, and has decided to wander the earth, seeking redemption. But he’s still reinterpreting a fictional Bible verse.) Proving this is as easy as grabbing a copy of the Bible and using book, chapter and verse to locate the actual psssage. In this case, since the quote is clearly supposed to be from the King James Version of the Bible, we just need to look it up in a KJV to find out what the actual verse says: “And I will execute great vengeance upon them with furious rebukes; and they shall know that I am the Lord, when I shall lay my vengeance upon them.” The “them” in this instance is not a reference to “the selfish and the tyranny of evil men,” but to the Philistines, a polytheistic people in Canaan who were constantly in conflict with the Israelites.(Quentin Tarantino was not going to let something Like a correct Bible verse get in the way of a good story.) You can still hear echoes of the real verse in the Jules Winfield monologue, of course, but there’s clearly a lot added into it to make it perfect for the moment in Pulp Fiction.111.3K views · View upvotes · View 7 shares · Submission accepted by · Answer requested by You can’t, as you’ve probably realised, because Tarantino heavily rewrote the quote to make it more badass-sounding. What Jules says is:The path of the righteous man is beset on all sides by the inequities of the selfish and the tyranny of evil men. Blessed is he who, in the name of charity and good will, shepherds the weak through the valley of the darkness. For he is truly his brother's keeper and the finder of lost children. And I will strike down upon thee with great vengeance and furious anger those who attempt to poison and destroy my brothers. And you will know I am the Lord when I lay my vengeance upon you.But Ezekiel 25:12–17, in the New International Version, actually goes like this:This is what the Sovereign Lord says: ‘Because Edom took revenge on Judah and became very guilty by doing so, therefore this is what the Sovereign Lord says: I will stretch out my hand against Edom and kill both man and beast. I will lay it waste, and from Teman to Dedan they will fall by the sword. I will take vengeance on Edom by the hand of my people Israel, and they will deal with Edom in accordance with my anger and my wrath; they will know my vengeance, declares the Sovereign Lord.’ This is what the Sovereign Lord says: ‘Because the Philistines acted in vengeance and took revenge with malice in their hearts, and with ancient hostility sought to destroy Judah, therefore this is what the Sovereign Lord says: I am about to stretch out my hand against the Philistines, and I will wipe out the Kerethites and destroy those remaining along the coast. I will carry out great vengeance on them and punish them in my wrath. Then they will know that I am the Lord, when I take vengeance on them.’Not quite as snappy as the Pulp Fiction version. Rather a lot of proper nouns. He also alluded to other well-known passages, such as Psalm 23:1–4:The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want. He maketh me to lie down in green pastures: he leadeth me beside the still waters. He restoreth my soul: he leadeth me in the paths of righteousness for his name's sake. Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me.And Genesis 4:9:And the LORD said unto Cain, Where is Abel thy brother? And he said, I know not: Am I my brother's keeper?Definitely one of the more snarky retorts to the Lord. Of course, Cain does know where Abel is: he’s just killed him.Question: Where can I find the exact reference in Ezekiel 25:17 that Jules Winnfield in Pulp Fiction quotes? Wow…these answers are all over the place. This is the original source of the quote:This is the beginning of the 1975 film The Bodyguard, starring martial arts legend Sonny Chiba. Here’s Ezekiel 25:17 (King James Version):It’s clear that Quentin Tarantino combined The Bodyguard intro with some of his own dialogue to create Jules speech in the film. Tarantino has explained this on multiple occasions in the past, and apparently the other people who answered this question didn’t see, nor read, any of those interviews,Nowhere, the verse in question is little to nothing like Jules’ speech in the movie. Here's the original verse in English and Hebrew:I will execute on them great acts of vengeance with furious punishments, and they will have to know that I am Jehovah when I bring my vengeance on them.וְעָשִׂ֤יתִי בָם֙ נְקָמֹ֣ות גְּדֹלֹ֔ות בְּתֹוכְחֹ֖ות חֵמָ֑ה וְיָֽדְעוּ֙ כִּֽי־אֲנִ֣י יְהוָ֔ה בְּתִתִּ֥י אֶת־נִקְמָתִ֖י בָּֽם׃ ס Here's Taratino's “expanded” version:“There’s a passage I got memorized. Ezekiel 25:17. “ “The path of the righteous man is beset on all sides by the inequities of the selfish and the tyranny of evil men. “ “Blessed is he who, in the name of charity and good will, shepherds the weak through the valley of the darkness, for he is truly his brother’s keeper and the finder of lost children and I will strike down upon thee with great vengeance and furious anger those who attempt to poison and destroy my brothers and you will know I am the Lord when I lay my vengeance upon you!”Tarantino's take on the verse in Ezekiel is like this gentleman's take on Jules Winnfield.Answered by · Author has 3K answers and 4.6M answer views · Jan 9, 2024The origin of that reference would be the script. That is to say, it’s not a direct quote of any actual Bible passage, and there’s of course a ton online as to whether it’s even a fair summary or extrapolation of what the book of Ezekiel was addressing in that section. Ezekiel 25 talks about the vengeance of God, but not about the path of the righteous man. It looks like the general understanding is it’s about God’s vengeance upon nations near Judah. Extending that too much to one’s own challenges and revenges (to say nothing of one’s own righteousness) is… a challenging bridge to successfully build.What is the line from Pulp Fiction that Samuel L Jackson uses where he includes the word smite?Smite?…No fucking clue. Unless it’s “Strike down upon thee with great vengeance and furious anger…” No, that ain’t it. I don’t know, probably somewhere in the car when I’m pissed off with John about the brains. I don’t know, fuck. Pulp Fiction nerds.Why did Jules say on Pulp Fiction, "My name's Pitt" when asked by Brett?“My name is Pitt, and your ass ain't talking your way outta this shit.” This was a pretty common thing in black neighborhoods when I was growing up. Phrases like, “My name is Bennet & and I ain't even in it.” Or “My name is Paul, and that's just between y'all” were said all the time. And it has nothing to with the person's actual name. Note that only the black characters say things like that. Jules & “Paul” definitely do it. Also note that the character we call “Paul” because he uses the Paul / y’all rhyme in the movie, in the screenplay, is actually called “English Dave.” English Dave is using the same rhyming device as Jules. Paul is not actually his name.ADDENDUM I just thought of another good one from my childhood, but it doesn't involve fake names (but almost). “This conversation is between A and B, so you should C your way out of it.”Why does Quentin Tarantino have a character in Pulp Fiction recite a fictional Biblical verse (Ezekiel 25-17)?Here is Quentin Tarantino’s own words about it from 1994. Hope it helps clear things up. QT: "This quote had a funny origin. ! heard it for the first time in a kung fu film, The Bodyguard (Tatsuichi Takamori, 1973}, where it appeared in the prologue. Then I located it in the Bible in 4 slightly different version. i'd also seen a Japanese ninja series on tv called Shadow Warriors (Fuii Tv 1960-85}, which Is the best cartoon i've seen on the screen. The action takes place in ancient Japan, between the good guys who want to open the country to Western influence and the bad guys who are isolationists.There's this group of ninjas who answer to no one and who, during theday, are complete imbeciles working as waiters in a restaueant, but at night, they are fearsome warriors At the end of each episode, there was a mortal Combat where the chief of the Shadow Warriors, before killing his adlversary, would make an interminable speech about the necessity for exterminating evil. The guy who had to listen to this speech was sure to die in the end! My friends and i were always fascinated by these endings, which we found cool and poetic. it was in this spirit that | put the quotation from ezekiel (25:17) in Jules mouth When | was writing the scenario, | realized that in the final scene in the coffe shop, Jules couldn't say this religious epiphany in the same way as he's said it before. After using it for ten years, for the first time he realizes what it really means. And that's the end of the film."Sponsored by Protect My FamilyReceive a complimentary Will Kit and Burial Guide for Veterans!Available to all Veterans and their families at no cost.Answered by · Author has 5.8K answers and 12M answer views · Jan 9, 2024If you’re looking for a reference to a place in the Bible, you’re never going to find it. Because the verse quoted in Pulp Fiction is entirely fictitious - it’s made up. It doesn’t exist anywhere in the Bible, and certainly not in Ezekiel 25:17, which actually reads: And I will execute great vengeance upon them with furious rebukes; and they shall know that I am the Lord, when I shall lay my vengeance upon them. Which are bad he is a bad guy… Why, Pete Hegseth used it and claimed it was front he Bible rather than a movie quote… it is the same justification.In the film Pulp Fiction, the character Jules reads a passage from the Bible to unfortunates that he is about to shoot dead. and they shall know that I am the LORD, when I shall lay my vengeance upon them.Why would Jules Winnfield, the hitman from "Pulp Fiction" reference the TV show "Happy Days" as if he spent days watching sit-coms when he wasn't killing people? Both Jules Winfield and Vincent Vega appear to be men in their mid 30s as does Ringo, Honey Bunny, Marcellus Wallace, Butch Coolidge, Winston Wolfe, Lance, Lance’s wife Jody, and Jimmie (Quentin Tarantino). Thirty-five year-olds in 1994 were 15 in 1974 thus the many 70s references. Plus both Happy Days and Kung Fu are and were seen in reruns in the 90s, albeit one more than the other. And Kool and the Gang gets played on old R&B stations all the time. Although 15 year-old hitmen, crime bosses, fixers/cleaners, drug dealers, armed robbers, and boxers are not uncommon; in the 1970s - they were very rare. I would imagine Tarentino took some liberties in his script though.What is the meaning behind Jules's Bible verse, "Thou shall not take the Lord's name in vain," in the film Pulp Fiction?It is the third of the Ten Commandments given to Moses 3400 years ago. A million Israelites had just had a miraculous deliverance from slavery, and were being led from Egypt to the promised land (what is now Israel and some surrounding areas). When the Israelites reached Mount Sinai God gave them ten moral laws which still apply today. The third is the verse you quoted. The commandment prohibits the misuse of the name of God. Anytime we use His name but don’t mean specifically to honor Him by our thoughts, words and actions, we misuse His name. His name can be misused many ways. Here are some:Like when a bride changes her name to her husband’s last name, we say she “takes” his name. Taking God’s name can be when a person says they believe in God, or calls themself a Christian or a Jew or a Muslim but they don’t live as God taught people to live. He said to “Love the Lord your God with all your heart.” When people say they believe in God but hate others, mistreat others, don’t love God, they take His name in vain. As a Christian, I believe that when someone says they believe in God but do not believe in Jesus or obey what He said to do, they take God’s name in vain.Using God’s name in an oath. “I swear to God I didn’t take the money!” Or “By God I’ll not put up with this any more!” He doesn’t like that.Using God’s name in a curse. “God damn you!” Or any use of the word goddamn. Or when we call a person “God-forsaken.” He doesn’t like that either.Even common expressions like “Oh my God!” or “Jesus H. Christ” or just the expression “Jesus” when we are exasperated - all these misuse God’s name. Anytime we utter the name of God in a way that does not honor Him is misusing His name. That’s what Jules was talking about when he stopped Vincent from blaspheming.Remember, in all of this, God cannot be manipulated, tricked, mocked, or bested with a technicality. If anyone says the name of God but does not love Him in their heart or wish Him honor, that person has taken the Lord’s name in vain.What is the Bible quote from Pulp Fiction?They "quote" Ezekiel 25:17, but it is really a made up quotation, it doesn't exist in the Bible. Tarantino is actually borrowing from a Sonny Chiba movie called The Bodyguard:As far as I can tell, the part that comes from Ezekiel is:“And I will execute great vengeance upon them with furious rebukes; and they shall know that I am the LORD, when I shall lay my vengeance upon them.”In the film Pulp Fiction, the character Jules reads a passage from the Bible to unfortunates that he is about to shoot dead. Where can I find the exact verbatim as read by Jules?It’s not a real Bible passage, although parts of it are from Ezekiel 25. It’s mostly Jules’s own mishmosh of muddled ideas about what he THINKS the Bible is about. His whole arc in the movie — which I consider the one morally redeeming part of an otherwise horrifically nihilistic film — is about realizing he’s wrong and he needs to change his life completely. Bible Gateway passage: Ezekiel 25 - King James VersionWhy does Quentin Tarantino have a character in Pulp Fiction recite a fictional Biblical verse (Ezekiel 25-17)?Question: Why, once and again, does Quentin Tarantino in Pulp Fiction recite a Biblical verse (Ezekiel 25-17) which, in reality, does not exist in that way? Umm…what difference does it make? The Christian Bible is often quoted incorrectly even by people who are trained scholars in the work. In this case Quentin Tarantino is not a biblical scholar, but a screenwriter who mixed portion of a bible verse with the narrative from the prologue of a 1970s Sonny Chiba martial arts film (The Bodyguard) The result was Jules’ lines in the film. There are no legal or even moral requirements to accurately quote the Bible or any other text. There might be an “ethical” requirement to do so if you are purporting that tome says something and then you quote incorrectly either by accident or by design. However, even that is a minor concern for the majority of people in the world who are adherents of a religion as they (sadly) would be unlikely to know the difference. BTW, here’s the Sonny Chiba prologue:Why would Jules Winnfield, the hitman from "Pulp Fiction" reference the TV show "Happy Days" as if he spent days watching sit-coms when he wasn't killing people? It seems odd.What is he supposed to do? Sit in a dark room? Meditate? Play with Legos? Being a hit man is not a 24/7 occupation. Maybe 2 days a month. They were “filling out the world”.What is the Bible verse that Samuel L. Jackson says in Pulp Fiction?Samuel L. Jackson's monologue with the alleged memorized bible quote before he and John Travolta violently kill the guy in the chair contains what is allegedly a quote from Ezekiel 25:17. Here is Ezekiel 25:17: And I will execute great vengeance upon them with furious rebukes; and they shall know that I am the LORD, when I shall lay my vengeance upon them. Ezekiel 25:17 What Samuel dramatically quotes as Ezekiel 25:17 is this: “The path of the righteous man is beset on all sides by the iniquities of the selfish and the tyranny of evil men. Blessed is he, who in the name of charity and good will, shepherds the weak through the valley of darkness, for he is truly his brother’s keeper and the finder of lost children. And I will strike down upon thee with great vengeance and furious anger those who would attempt to poison and destroy my brothers. And you will know my name is the Lord when I lay my vengeance upon thee.” The ending is almost a verbatim quote from Ezekiel 25:17. The rest leading up to that is a hodge-podge of biblical language strung together like a beat poet at a slam: a Frankenstein verse if you will, stitched together from a number of different places. Chilling. Powerful. Fiction at its best. You might like this link where the author tries to piece together the various bible verses the script writer kind of pieces together for this scene: The Truth on Pulp Fiction Ezekiel 25:17 Samuel L. Jackson Bible Quote Author Edit 12/12/24 - as of Dec 2025 the link above is valid again but just in case it ever goes away again here is the paragraph that directly addresses where the various other words in the line from Pulp Fiction may have come from: Pretty much all of the themes Jackson’s passage incorporates are found in different places in the Bible, but they are all re-workings, not true to the original text. The portion of the monologue about the tyranny of evil men is inspired by Ezekiel 34. The portion about the valley of darkness refers to King David’s words in Psalm 23, and the portion about being one’s brother’s keeper refers to the first human death, occurring in Genesis 4, in which Cain, after murdering his brother, asks the LORD, “Am I my brother’s keeper?” - taken from a blog post by Chad Hussey on Nov 27th, 2013 on the website truthbygrace dot org.
